intro: で marks the setting an action works through: the stage it happens on, the tool or route it uses, the stuff it is made from, the circumstance that brings it about, the frame a comparison or a count is made in, and the time or amount it takes. Picture a frame drawn around an action: で labels the frame, never the target. If the noun is where something goes, where something simply is, or what the verb acts on, it is not で.

skills.rule: The place where an action is carried out takes で; the place where something exists or ends up takes に.
skills.explain:
Put で after a place when something is done there: 図書館で勉強する (study at the library), 駅で待つ (wait at the station), 家で晩ご飯を食べる (eat dinner at home). The verb is an activity, and the place is just its stage.

に marks a different relationship: where something is (ある, いる), where someone lives (住む), and the point something lands on (座る, 置く, 書く, 乗る). Compare 公園にいる (be in the park) with 公園で遊ぶ (play in the park). The same noun takes different particles depending on the verb, so look at the verb, not the place.

One trap: events. ある takes に for things, but で when the subject is an event: 会議は三階である (the meeting is held on the third floor). Another: 働く takes で (会社で働く), but 勤める takes に (会社に勤める).

examples.jp: 図書館[としょかん]{で}勉強[べんきょう]します。
examples.en: I study at the library.

examples.jp: 駅[えき]{で}友達[ともだち]を待[ま]ちました。
examples.en: I waited for a friend at the station.

examples.jp: 子供[こども]たちが公園[こうえん]{で}遊[あそ]んでいます。
examples.en: The children are playing in the park.

examples.jp: どこ{で}その傘[かさ]を買[か]ったんですか。
examples.en: Where did you buy that umbrella?

examples.jp: 明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]は三階[さんがい]{で}あります。
examples.en: Tomorrow's meeting is on the third floor.

contrast.note: に marks where something is (部屋にいる), where you live (大阪に住む) or where something is put or arrives (机に置く). Use で only when the verb is an activity done at the place.
を with a place marks ground you move through or leave: 公園を歩く (walk through the park), 道を渡る. 公園で歩く means walking around inside the park as an activity. Both are correct; the particle sets the meaning.

mistakes.bad: 図書館[としょかん]{に}勉強[べんきょう]します。
mistakes.good: 図書館[としょかん]{で}勉強[べんきょう]します。
mistakes.note: Studying is an activity, so its location takes で, not に.

mistakes.bad: 東京[とうきょう]{で}住[す]んでいます。
mistakes.good: 東京[とうきょう]{に}住[す]んでいます。
mistakes.note: 住む treats the place as where you are, so it takes に.

mistakes.bad: パーティーはホテル{に}あります。
mistakes.good: パーティーはホテル{で}あります。
mistakes.note: When the thing that 'is' somewhere is an event, ある takes で.

skills.tip: Ask: is someone doing something there? Doing takes で; being or landing takes に.

skills.rule: The tool, vehicle, language or method you do something with takes で.
skills.explain:
で marks the means: whatever the action goes through to get done. Tools (箸で食べる, ペンで書く), transport (バスで行く, 自転車で来る), language (日本語で話す), media and methods (電話で話す, メールで送る, カードで払う). In English this is 'with', 'by' or 'in', and all three are で when they name an instrument.

The main confusion is English 'with'. When 'with' means a companion, it is と: 友達と行く (go with a friend). When it means an instrument, it is で: ナイフで切る (cut with a knife).

For going on foot, Japanese uses the verb 歩いて行く (or the noun 徒歩で), never 足で行く. And transport verbs split: 電車で行く (go by train) uses で, but 電車に乗る (get on the train) uses に, because the train is where you land.

examples.jp: 箸[はし]{で}食[た]べます。
examples.en: I eat with chopsticks.

examples.jp: 毎日[まいにち]バス{で}学校[がっこう]へ行[い]きます。
examples.en: I go to school by bus every day.

examples.jp: 日本語[にほんご]{で}話[はな]してください。
examples.en: Please speak in Japanese.

examples.jp: 写真[しゃしん]はメール{で}送[おく]りました。
examples.en: I sent the photos by email.

examples.jp: カード{で}払[はら]ってもいいですか。
examples.en: May I pay by card?

contrast.note: と is 'with' a partner (母と作った, made it with my mother); で is 'with' a tool (はさみで切った, cut it with scissors). If the noun could thank you, it is と.
に marks the vehicle you board (バスに乗る); で marks the vehicle as your means of travel (バスで行く).
日本語を話す means you speak the language (as a skill); 日本語で話す means you talk using Japanese. Both are correct but say different things.

mistakes.bad: ナイフ{と}切[き]りました。
mistakes.good: ナイフ{で}切[き]りました。
mistakes.note: A knife is an instrument, not a companion: で.

mistakes.bad: 電車[でんしゃ]{に}会社[かいしゃ]へ行[い]きます。
mistakes.good: 電車[でんしゃ]{で}会社[かいしゃ]へ行[い]きます。
mistakes.note: The train is how you travel here, so で. に goes with 乗る.

mistakes.bad: 足[あし]{で}駅[えき]まで行[い]きました。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いて行[い]きました。
mistakes.note: 'On foot' is 歩いて, not 足で.

skills.tip: Can you add 'using' in English? 'Using a pen', 'using the bus', 'using Japanese': then it is で.

skills.rule: What something is made of takes で.
skills.explain:
With 作る, できている and similar verbs, で marks the material or ingredients: 木で作った箱 (a box made of wood), 卵で作る (make with eggs), この家は石でできている (this house is made of stone). It is the means idea again: the material is what you make the thing with.

から also marks material, and the textbook line is this: use で when the material can still be seen in the result (wood in a wooden chair), and から when it has been transformed beyond recognition (お酒は米から作る, sake is made from rice). Native speakers do not always keep to this line, but it is the safe default.

Do not confuse the verb phrase with a noun label. 木の机 (a wooden desk) uses の, because it just describes the desk. 木で作った机 (a desk made of wood) uses で, because it modifies the verb 作った.
patterns: [thing] は [material] で できている

examples.jp: この箱[はこ]は木[き]{で}作[つく]りました。
examples.en: I made this box out of wood.

examples.jp: 紙[かみ]{で}飛行機[ひこうき]を作[つく]りましょう。
examples.en: Let's make a plane out of paper.

examples.jp: この人形[にんぎょう]は布[ぬの]{で}できています。
examples.en: This doll is made of cloth.

examples.jp: 昨日[きのう]、残[のこ]った野菜[やさい]{で}スープを作[つく]った。
examples.en: Yesterday I made soup with the leftover vegetables.

contrast.note: から is for raw material changed past recognition: 味噌は大豆から作る (miso is made from soybeans). If you can see the material in the result, use で.
の labels a noun directly (紙のコップ, a paper cup). With a verb like 作る or できている, the material takes で.

mistakes.bad: 紙[かみ]{に}鶴[つる]を作[つく]りました。
mistakes.good: 紙[かみ]{で}鶴[つる]を作[つく]りました。
mistakes.note: The paper is the material, not a location: で.

mistakes.bad: この机[つくえ]は木[き]{を}できています。
mistakes.good: この机[つくえ]は木[き]{で}できています。
mistakes.note: できている takes no object; the material takes で.

skills.tip: 'Made of X' or 'made with X' and you can still see X: X で.

skills.rule: A noun that causes an event takes で: 病気で, 雪で, 事故で.
skills.explain:
Put で after a noun naming a cause, and the clause after it names the result: 風邪で学校を休んだ (I missed school because of a cold), 雪で電車が止まった (the trains stopped because of the snow), 事故で遅れた (I was late because of an accident). Typical causes are illness, weather, accidents, noise and busy periods.

This で attaches to a noun. For a whole clause, use から or ので: 雪が降ったので (because it snowed). And because で reads as a plain circumstance, the result is usually something that happened, not a choice you are urging. With requests, invitations and orders, use から or ので.

Do not confuse it with に after emotion verbs. 大きい音にびっくりした (I was startled by the loud noise) uses に, because the noise is the thing reacted to.

examples.jp: 風邪[かぜ]{で}学校[がっこう]を休[やす]みました。
examples.en: I missed school because of a cold.

examples.jp: 雪[ゆき]{で}電車[でんしゃ]が止[と]まりました。
examples.en: The trains stopped because of the snow.

examples.jp: 事故[じこ]{で}道[みち]が混[こ]んでいます。
examples.en: The road is jammed because of an accident.

examples.jp: 大雨[おおあめ]{で}試合[しあい]が中止[ちゅうし]になりました。
examples.en: The match was called off because of the heavy rain.

examples.jp: 地震[じしん]{で}家[いえ]が壊[こわ]れました。
examples.en: The house was destroyed in the earthquake.

contrast.note: から follows a clause (雨が降ったから) and can back a request: 雨だから傘を持って行って. A bare cause noun before a result takes で.
に marks what you react to with surprise, joy or fear (知らせに驚いた). で marks what brings about an event (台風で木が倒れた).

mistakes.bad: 風邪[かぜ]{から}休[やす]みました。
mistakes.good: 風邪[かぜ]{で}休[やす]みました。
mistakes.note: A bare noun as cause takes で; から needs a clause such as 風邪をひいたから.

mistakes.bad: 台風[たいふう]{が}飛行機[ひこうき]が遅[おく]れました。
mistakes.good: 台風[たいふう]{で}飛行機[ひこうき]が遅[おく]れました。
mistakes.note: The typhoon is the cause, not the subject: で.

skills.tip: Noun + で + what happened = 'because of noun'. A whole clause instead? Switch to から or ので.

skills.rule: The range a superlative is judged in, or the group that does something together, takes で.
skills.explain:
First use: the frame for 'the most'. 世界で一番高い山 (the tallest mountain in the world), クラスで一番背が高い (the tallest in the class), 果物の中でりんごが一番好き (of all fruit, I like apples best). The range is the set you compare within, and it takes で.

Second use: number and group words that describe how many act as a unit. 三人で行く (go as a group of three), 一人で住む (live alone), みんなで歌う (sing all together), 家族で旅行する (travel as a family). Compare 三人と行く, which means going with three other people.

Third use: totals. 全部で千円です (it comes to one thousand yen in total), 二つで五百円 (five hundred yen for two). The count or set is the frame the price is stated in.

examples.jp: 一人[ひとり]{で}来[き]ました。
examples.en: I came by myself.

examples.jp: 全部[ぜんぶ]{で}千円[せんえん]です。
examples.en: It comes to a thousand yen altogether.

examples.jp: 週末[しゅうまつ]は家族[かぞく]{で}旅行[りょこう]します。
examples.en: At the weekend we're going on a family trip.

examples.jp: 富士山[ふじさん]は日本[にほん]{で}一番[いちばん]高[たか]い山[やま]です。
examples.en: Mount Fuji is the highest mountain in Japan.

examples.jp: スポーツの中[なか]{で}何[なに]が一番[いちばん]好[す]きですか。
examples.en: Of all sports, which do you like best?

contrast.note: 日本の山 just labels the mountains as Japan's. The standard way to set the range a 一番 is judged in is で: 日本で一番高い山, クラスで一番速い.
三人と行く: you go with three others. 三人で行く: three people go, you included.
に cannot mark a comparison range. クラスに一番 is wrong; say クラスで一番.

mistakes.bad: クラス{に}一番[いちばん]背[せ]が高[たか]いです。
mistakes.good: クラス{で}一番[いちばん]背[せ]が高[たか]いです。
mistakes.note: The group you compare within takes で.

mistakes.bad: 一人[ひとり]{に}映画[えいが]を見[み]に行[い]きました。
mistakes.good: 一人[ひとり]{で}映画[えいが]を見[み]に行[い]きました。
mistakes.note: 'By oneself' is 一人で. に cannot mark how many people act.

skills.tip: 'In the world', 'of all', 'as a group of three', 'in total': each is a frame, so each is で.

skills.rule: The time or amount something takes takes で: 一時間で終わる, 千円で買える.
skills.explain:
で after a length of time means 'in' or 'within': 一時間で終わる (finish in an hour), 三日で読んだ (read it in three days), 駅まで五分で着く (get to the station in five minutes). The span is the budget the action is completed in. A clock time is different: 三時に終わる (finish at three) takes に.

The same idea applies to cost: 千円で買える (you can buy it for a thousand yen).

で also marks an end point: これで終わりです (that's the end, with this), 今日で最後です (today is the last day), 今月で辞めます (I'm leaving at the end of this month). Read it as 'with this, the count is complete'.

Keep the frequency に apart: 一週間に二回 (twice a week) is a rate. 一週間で読んだ (read it in a week) is a span.

examples.jp: これ{で}終[お]わりです。
examples.en: That's all; we're done.

examples.jp: 駅[えき]まで五分[ごふん]{で}着[つ]きます。
examples.en: You get to the station in five minutes.

examples.jp: この本[ほん]は三日[みっか]{で}読[よ]みました。
examples.en: I read this book in three days.

examples.jp: このシャツは千円[せんえん]{で}買[か]えます。
examples.en: You can buy this shirt for a thousand yen.

examples.jp: アルバイトは今月[こんげつ]{で}辞[や]めます。
examples.en: I'm quitting my part-time job at the end of this month.

contrast.note: に marks a point (三時に終わる) or a rate (一日に三回). A span you finish within takes で (三時間で終わる).
まで means 'until' (五時まで働く); までに means 'by' (五時までに出す). 一時間で means 'taking an hour'.

mistakes.bad: 宿題[しゅくだい]は一時間[いちじかん]{に}終[お]わりました。
mistakes.good: 宿題[しゅくだい]は一時間[いちじかん]{で}終[お]わりました。
mistakes.note: An hour is a span here, not a clock time: で.

mistakes.bad: 今日[きょう]{まで}最後[さいご]です。
mistakes.good: 今日[きょう]{で}最後[さいご]です。
mistakes.note: 'Today is the last day' marks an end point with で.

skills.tip: Clock time: に. Length of time or a price: で. If English says 'in an hour' or 'for a thousand yen', use で.
